item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves will host the Philadelphia Phillies in a decisive Game Three of the National League Wild Card series tonight (Thursday, October 1). The winner will advance to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Division Series (NLDS). The Braves won Game One, but the Phillies rallied to win Game Two on Wednesday (September 30), setting the stage for this winner-take-all contest.
The game will start at 8 p.m. ET and will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock. Spanish language coverage will be available on Universo and Univision Radio, while ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games.
The Phillies' starting pitcher remains undecided, with options including Aaron Nola and ace Zack Wheeler. Meanwhile, the Braves may rely on Grant Holmes to handle the bulk of the innings, though they have not confirmed if he will start or follow an opener. Left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter are potential openers.
Both teams have key players to watch. For the Phillies, Alec Bohm hit a game-winning homer in Game Two, while Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie the game. On the Braves' side, Michael Harris II and Mauricio Dubón have been performing well at the plate.
The Phillies have a history of postseason success against the Braves, having defeated them in previous playoff series, including the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS. The outcome of tonight's game will determine who advances to face the Dodgers in the next round.

item.content:encoded:
October baseball is upon us, and we have a massive playoff game on Thursday night.
The Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves are the only teams remaining in the wild card round, setting up a standalone Game 3 on Thursday night.
The Phillies came back from a 3-1 deficit in Game 2 – after a key Bryce Harper error – to win in extra innings behind solo shots from Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Alec Bohm.
The starting pitching matchup for Game 3 is murky at the moment, although two beat reporters gave some insight into what these teams might do.
Long-time Phillies reporter Jim Salisbury shared that he’s hearing veteran Aaron Nola will get the start for the Phillies while the Braves will go with an opener in Ray Kerr. The Atlanta bullpen is elite, ranking fourth in MLB in ERA during the regular season.
Braves beat reporter Mark Bowman also shared some insight to the starting pitching matchup, mentioning that Braves righty Grant Holmes could be used as the “bulk” option behind Kerr on Thursday. He also believes the Phillies will use a combo of Nola and ace Zack Wheeler, who would be pitching on short rest after leading the Phillies to a win on Sunday.
All hands are going to be on deck in this matchup for both teams, as this is a win-or-go-home scenario.
Oddsmakers have set the Phillies as slight favorites on the road, a sign that they have more confidence in Philly’s options to start in this game.
Here’s a breakdown of the odds, a player prop to bet and my prediction for Thursday’s Game 3.

- Braves +1.5 (-174)

Phillies vs. Braves Best MLB Prop bets
Braves Best MLB Prop Bet
- Drake Baldwin OVER 1.5 Hits, Runs, RBIs (-108)
In today’s edition of Walk-Off Wagers – our MLB Best Bets column at SI – I shared why Baldwin is worth a look if Nola gets the start:
If Nola ends up getting the start, it’s a good sign for Braves catcher/designated hitter Drake Baldwin.
Baldwin picked up two hits and a run batted in on Wednesday, and he’s fared extremely well against Nola in his career.
The 25-year-old is 5-for-11 (.455) against Nola in his career, with a .955 OPS. He’s driven in one run against the Phillies veteran, and Nola has struggled quite a bit with the long ball this season, allowing 37 in 33 starts during the regular season.
A homer would immediately hit this prop for Baldwin, and he’s coming off a strong showing on Wednesday. During the regular season, the Braves star hit .284 overall and .307 against right-handed pitching.
Baldwin also entered the playoffs on a hot streak, batting .360 with two home runs, five runs batted in and a .951 OPS over the final two weeks (12 games). He’s a pretty interesting bet with this prop set at -108 on Thursday.
Phillies vs. Braves Prediction and Pick
Another play from today’s Walk-Off Wagers, I’m going to back the Phillies to win and advance after stealing Game 2:
There’s certainly an argument to be made for the Braves, who went 23 games over .500 at home in the regular season, but I lean with the Phillies in Game 3.
If Wheeler is able to pitch on short rest in any capacity, he’ll be by far the best pitcher in this game and had a massive finish to the regular season. Wheeler had a 1.71 ERA in September, lowering his season-long ERA to 3.00. He may not be able to give the Phils a ton of length, but it should help ease the pressure on their bullpen.
Nola has pitched in a ton of big games in his career, and I don’t want to downplay his two solid starts against Atlanta earlier this month. In two outings, Nola allowed just 10 hits and three earned runs across 13.1 innings of work.
The Braves have only used Kerr as an opener once this season, and Holmes had some very shaky advanced numbers in the regular season, ranking in the 12th percentile in expected ERA and the 18th percentile in expected BAA.
The Atlanta bullpen has been taxed in this series, pitching Didier Fuentes, Dylan Lee and Rasiel Iglesias in back-to-back days. That’s not nothing. Can the Atlanta ‘pen hold up after blowing Game 2?
I’d much rather take the Phillies and their proven veteran starters in a winner-take-all game, especially after they showed they can power themselves to a win on Wednesday.
Pick: Phillies Moneyline (-118 at DraftKings)

item.title: [mix1063.com] White Sox pounce early, finish sweep of Astros for first playoff series win since 2005 | Mix 106.3 – Jonesboro, AR

item.content:encoded:
By KRISTIE RIEKEN AP Sports Writer
HOUSTON (AP) — From 100 losses to their first playoff series win in two decades, these scrappy Chicago White Sox just keep outdoing themselves.
The White Sox used a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday to sweep their AL Wild Card Series.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them as they’re probably the only ones in this country that believed that they could be in this spot,” manager Will Venable said. “And they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that, and they made it happen. So it’s awesome to get to this point.”
It’s the first time Chicago has won a playoff series since beating Houston in the World Series in 2005. Under the direction of Venable, the second-year skipper, and with a letter of support from Pope Leo XIV, the White Sox advanced to face AL Central champion Cleveland in the AL Division Series beginning Saturday in Cleveland.
“It means everything for our fans,” Meidroth said. “They have been incredible all year. So the main thing was getting back to Chicago for some postseason baseball, and so we’re really blessed that we get to do that.”
The White Sox, who lost 100 games in each of the last three seasons, are the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth.
The AL West-winning Astros went 81-81 to become the first team to reach the postseason without a winning record. Their recent playoff woes in Houston continued Wednesday as they dropped their ninth straight home playoff game in a ninth trip to the postseason in the last 10 years.
Chicago pounced on the Astros for four runs in the first inning a day after scoring three in the first two innings of a 6-3 win. Houston ace Hunter Brown was lifted after getting just two outs and wasn’t helped by a sloppy defense which committed two first-inning errors.
He was 6-0 with a 2.39 ERA in six career starts against the White Sox before Wednesday’s debacle.
The Astros clawed their way back into it with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve to trail by 1 entering the sixth inning.
AJ Blubaugh, who opened Game 1, and Peter Lambert, pitching on two days’ rest, combined to retire the next 13 batters after Brown exited. Chicago’s next baserunner came when Lambert walked Andrew Benintendi to start the sixth and then walked Tristan Peters.
Bryan Abreu came in, and Meidroth smashed his fifth pitch off the wall in left field to push the lead to 7-3. He yelled on his entire trip around the bases to the delight of a patch of White Sox fans seated near the visitor’s dugout.
“I was looking for something middle up,” Meidroth said. “He’s had my number all year, really good fastball, so I got something middle up and I was able to cash in for the team. So, yeah, that was awesome.”
Houston faced boos for a second game in a row from an unusually thin crowd. It’s a second straight playoff trip where the Astros have been swept at home in the wild card after losing both games to Detroit in 2024.
Now they’ll face an uncertain future with manager Joe Espada’s contract set to expire at season’s end after general manager Dana Brown was fired last month.
“We fought back and we set our goal to win this division and we accomplished that,” Espada said. “We wanted to play deep in October. We came short on that. But just the way our guys stayed together and were able to get this far, extremely proud of our team.”
It was a disappointing series for Houston slugger and AL MVP-favorite Yordan Alvarez, who managed only a single with two strikeouts in eight at-bats in the series.
Altuve’s shot to the seats in left field in the fourth inning got the Astros within 4-3. It was the 28th postseason homer of his career, which is second in MLB history behind Manny Ramirez (29).
“We’re all sad,” Altuve said. “We wanted to go to the World Series and win it. But today is sorrow for the final day of the season.”
The Astros had a shot to take the lead before Meidroth’s homer. They loaded the bases with two outs in the fifth, but Anthony Kay retired Altuve on a fly out to end the inning.
___

item.content:encoded:
October 01, 2026
It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night.
Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure.
Before Game 3's first pitch, we have a few Phillies' thoughts we'd like to share:
How are we feeling about Aaron Nola — named Game 3's starter earlier Thursday morning? In his 15 starts prior to last Saturday's bizarre three run first inning and out for the Phillies' veteran, Nola boasted a pretty solid 3.12 ERA which is more in line with the Nola who got a monster free agent contract a few offseasons ago.
He's also got some postseason pedigree. He's started 11 playoff games over the last five Octobers, and his two worst starts actually came during the World Series run in 2022. In six starts since 2023, he has a 3.00 ERA and 3-2 record. Is he better than Zack Wheeler pitching on three days rest for the first time ever? The Phils coaching staff made their choice and it's a reasonable one, if nothing else.
If Alec Bohm is parting ways with the Phillies in a few weeks — his contract is set to expire and the Phillies are likely to let him walk and give top prospect Aidan Miller the chance to start the season at third (or second) in 2027 — he gave Phillies fans a spectacular parting gift.
ALEC BOHM GO-AHEAD HOMER
PHILLIES LEAD IN THE 10TH 🤯 pic.twitter.com/S4wFOFyDq1
By virtue of all three other Wild Card series' wrapping up (more on that in a second), the Phillies have Thursday all to themselves and have moved from a 2 p.m. start to prime time (at 8:15 on NBC).
The Phillies are no strangers to primetime playoff starts — they've had a ton of them over the last half decade. They also play better at night. Their win percentage under the lights (55.5%, 61-49) is better than during the afternoon (51%, 26-25). With some extra time for their pitchers to rest and prepare, this is probably a net positive move for the Phillies.
As we just mentioned, the other three series' ended with a 2-0 sweep. Since the league switched to the three-game Wild Card first round format, teams who win Game 1 are now 24-3. The Phillies have a chance to be the fourth.
Philadelphia also has the chance to be the first team in franchise history to win a playoff series (albeit a short one) after losing a Game 1. They are 0-9 historically when they start a series off with a loss.
Another mark, probably, in the Phillies' advantage column is that they're going up against a Braves team unprepared to send a third starter out there. Lefty reliever Ray Kerr — with an impressive 1.77 ERA this season — is going to start the game, likely to face the lefty-heavy front of the Phillies order (Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber). Perhaps the Phillies should consider splitting these hitters up and having Schwarber bat lead off, with Trea Turner second and Harper third?
After Kerr, it's expected the Braves will go to righty starter Grant Holmes, who has a 3.44 ERA this season. Holmes faced the Phillies four times during the regular season and the Phils' hitters will all have recent recollections of facing him.
The Phillies will see how far they can get behind Nola, but it'll be interesting to see who's the next man in. Will it be Jesús Luzardo who pitched in Game 1? Will they ultimately call on Wheeler (or optimistically save him for an NLDS Game 1)? Can Andrew Painter throw on back-to-back days?

item.dc:creator: Matt Yoder
item.description: Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. And who wouldn’t want to celebrate with John Fanta? The San Diego Padres were the last team to celebrate late Wednesday night, sweeping the Chicago Cubs in two games to win their Wild Card series. And much like we saw in Chicago with the White Sox and in New York with the Yankees, there were festive scenes. And
item.content:encoded:
Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. And who wouldn’t want to celebrate with John Fanta?
The San Diego Padres were the last team to celebrate late Wednesday night, sweeping the Chicago Cubs in two games to win their Wild Card series. And much like we saw in Chicago with the White Sox and in New York with the Yankees, there were festive scenes. And while nobody quite did it like Muretaka Murakami with the South Siders, the Padres at least had NBC’s energetic and affable reporter/host/announcer in their clubhouse.
Fanta interviewed Padres superstar Fernando Tatis Jr. in the locker room and asked about how the team found their groove after a mediocre first 100 games of the season. He also asked Tatis to look ahead to the challenge of facing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS and ace pitcher Jacob Misiorowski.
But honestly, all we wanted to see was John Fanta get doused with some kind of alcoholic beverage. And that’s what Tatis delivered. A bottle of Bud Light was the shower of choice. Thankfully, Fanta was wearing a clear plastic parka because he knew what was coming, too.
A conversation and a Bud Light shower with Fernando Tatis Jr.
The San Diego Padres are rolling on to Milwaukee. pic.twitter.com/LVyKbvxvIS
— John Fanta (@John_Fanta) October 1, 2026
We have certainly come a long way since the days when Tim McCarver and Deion Sanders shared a tense moment with the Atlanta Braves all those years ago, when he got his own bath in the locker room.

item.content:encoded:
Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

The Padres clubhouse, naturally, was full of celebrations — including one featuring owner Kwanza Jones and Fernando Tatis Jr. Jones celebrated with the players following the team’s victory over Chicago, wearing ski goggles and popping bottles of champagne. item.content:encoded:
San Diego stayed hot against the Cubs in the wild-card series, sweeping Chicago in two games to advance. The Padres clubhouse, naturally, was full of celebrations — including one featuring owner Kwanza Jones and Fernando Tatis Jr.
Jones celebrated with the players following the team’s victory over Chicago, wearing ski goggles and popping bottles of champagne.
Jones, and her husband, Jose E. Feliciano purchased the Padres for $3.9 billion from the Seidler family in August.
The couple held an official introductory press conference at the end of August, where Jones promised the team would “win it all” in the foreseeable future. Thus far, the Padres have come out roaring in the postseason.
San Diego scored 12 runs in two games against the Cubs, while the Padres pitching staff limited Chicago to a single run throughout the wild-card series.
“It’s another step,” Jones said. “It’s not the end of the journey it’s a continuation.”
The next step for San Diego will be facing the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers. If the Padres bats stay hot and the pitching staff remains sharp, there’s a good chance the rest of the playoffs run through San Diego.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

So lit, in fact, that team owner Kwanza Jones was cutting it up with the rest of the team. Video shared on social media by reporter Marty Caswell shows San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. dancing with Kwanza Jones during the team’s locker room celebration after the Padres swept the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night. item.content:encoded:
The postgame celebrations in the San Diego Padres’ locker room after beating the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card game were absolutely lit. So lit, in fact, that team owner Kwanza Jones was cutting it up with the rest of the team.
Video shared on social media by reporter Marty Caswell shows San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. dancing with Kwanza Jones during the team’s locker room celebration after the Padres swept the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night.
Padres owner Kwanza Jones joined Fernando Tatis Jr. in popping bottles and dancing in the clubhouse after San Diego swept the Cubs
I never completed this interview with Kwanza Jones, thanks to @tatis_jr
@@FriarTerritory pic.twitter.com/kxmqAmsH3o
— Marty Caswell (@MartyCaswell) October 1, 2026
Why yes, Fernando Tatís danced with Kwanza Jones pic.twitter.com/E993DYRC78
— Marty Caswell (@MartyCaswell) October 1, 2026
Tatis finished the Wild Card Series against the Cubs 2-for-7 with one home run, one RBI, three runs scored, one walk and one stolen base.
Jones and her husband, José E. Feliciano, were unanimously approved by MLB owners on Aug. 17 in a $3.9 billion deal, the richest franchise sale in league history. Jones is MLB’s first Black woman majority owner, while Feliciano serves as the team’s control person under league rules.
When the Padres clinched a playoff spot at Dodger Stadium on September 24, Tatis danced on the infield grass and hugged Jones, while a video of Feliciano chugging a beer bong with pitcher Walker Buehler went viral on social media.
The Padres closed out the Cubs with a 4-1 win in Game 2 at Petco Park, finishing a sweep after surging through September as one of baseball’s hottest teams. The NLDS against Milwaukee starts Saturday night.
With their win over the Cubs in the NL Wild Card Round, the Padres have advanced to the National League Divisional Series, where they’ll take on the Brewers. The series will kick off in Milwaukee with Game 1 on Saturday, October 3.

item.title: [heavy.com] Is Zack Wheeler Available? Phillies' Pitching Plan Revealed Behind Aaron Nola
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line. It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on. item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line.
It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on.
Both teams entered Thursday with a bit of uncertainty about their pitching plans, but things are beginning to take shape.
According to multiple reports, the Phillies will be starting the veteran Aaron Nola on the mound. It was the most logical decision given that he’s on full rest.
It does raise the question about Zack Wheeler, though. He hasn’t pitched in this series. Would the Phillies really go out of the postseason potentially without even using him?
There’s reason to expect that Wheeler could follow Nola at some point in Thursday’s game.
Is Zack Wheeler Available?
Wheeler is available on Thursday night, according to The Athletic’s Matt Gelb.
“Nola will be on regular rest after pitching most recently in the penultimate game of the regular season Saturday, when he opened a bullpen game on two days’ rest and only threw 21 pitches,” Gelb writes. “The Phillies could also use Zack Wheeler, who is on three days’ rest, as a reliever in Game 3. Jesús Luzardo, who started Game 1 on Tuesday, is in play for an inning or two in Game 3 if needed.”
Wheeler pitched the Phillies’ regular season finale on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Philadelphia needed to win that game to ensure a playoff spot, and they did, so Wheeler’s arm was used for a good cause there.
Generally, starting pitchers then get at least four days of rest after an outing.
If Wheeler were to pitch Thursday, he would’ve gotten three days of rest — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Plenty of pitchers go on shorter rest in the playoffs, but it still comes with a risk. It throws off between-start routines and has potentially a greater injury probability.
A pitcher may also be slightly less effective if their arm isn’t feeling as fresh and rested as usual.
Wheeler, though, is one of this era’s great pitchers and had a 3.00 ERA in 28 outings in the regular season for the Phillies. He’s 36 years old now and doesn’t have a ton of time left in his career, most likely. He’d be a logical guy to trust in a big spot on Thursday night.
Of course, if the Phillies were able to win without using Wheeler, he could start Game 1 of the NLDS on Saturday. But that only matters if the Phillies get there.
Zack Wheeler Short Rest History
According to John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia, Wheeler has pitched in relief on short rest once in his career.
That was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS. The Phillies were eliminated that night, 4-2, by the Diamondbacks.
Wheeler did his part, though. He went 1.2 innings out of the pen, striking out one and walking one while not allowing a hit or a run.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Phillies reportedly make Game 3 starter decision between Aaron Nola and Zack Wheeler | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive. Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies? According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phil
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive.
Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies?
According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phillies have made their decision between Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. The resurgent Nola will get the Game 3 start, as the Phillies hope to clinch Thursday night in Atlanta.
Phillies turn to Aaron Nola for Game 3 vs. Braves
"Hearing Phillies will start Aaron Nola tonight vs. Braves opener Ray Kerr, a lefty," Salisbury reports. "Always subject to change but that's the plan as of this AM."
The Phillies' plan for the winner-takes-all Game 3 of the NL Wild Card series against the Braves will be to start Nola instead of Wheeler on short rest.
While having Wheeler go would've been preferred, if there was ever a time to trust in Nola, it's this season after his second-half resurgence.
As June came to a close, his 6.04 ERA had Phillies fans, rightfully, very concerned about his massive contract going forward.
But his final 11 starts of the 2026 season resulted in an incredible 2.93 ERA. While some luck has gone his way during that stretch, his massive improvement is giving the Phillies enough confidence to turn to him for Game 3.
On the other side, the Braves are reportedly going to start Ray Kerr, a left-handed pitcher, as potentially an opener until they turn the reins over to Grant Holmes.
The Phillies have Wheeler as an option out of the bullpen for multiple innings in Game 3, but ideally they'll ride Nola for as long as possible.
If they could somehow win without pitching Wheeler, that would be the best-case scenario. The same goes for both Jesus Luzardo and Andrew Painter, both of whom would be willing to pitch in Game 3 if needed.
With how shaky the bullpen is, the Phillies are really going to need Nola to go deep into this game, unless the Phillies' offense comes alive and blows this game out of proportion, and some normal relievers can come into the game without worry of blowing it.
But the most important thing is how Nola performs, as he's expected to get the ball to start the game. It's the right call, especially considering how he's on normal rest and is more ready to go than any other pitcher on the roster.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox Trade Plans for Jarren Duran Revealed
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

item.title: [New York Daily News] With dad on hand, Cody Bellinger delivers his own big Yankees moment: ‘He’s built for this’
item.dc:creator: Peter Sblendorio
item.description: The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove. In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001. But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention. Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to
item.content:encoded:
The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove.
In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001.
But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention.
Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to the ALDS.
“I’m able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said afterward, reflecting on sharing the night with his father. “That was a cool moment, just a great game. Happy I was able to contribute, and we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Continued contributions from Bellinger would go a long way in the Yankees making a deep postseason run, with the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays up next in the ALDS.
Bellinger takes on added importance with Aaron Judge sidelined indefinitely due to a calf strain.
He was one of the driving forces in the Yankees’ two-day demolition of the archrival Red Sox, whom they outscored 18-2. The All-Star went 3-for-8 in the series and delivered a pair of key hits in Wednesday’s clincher.
With Yankees leading by a run in the fifth inning, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy controversially removed right-handed starter Sonny Gray after 70 pitches with runners at the corners and two outs.
Tracy turned to the left-handed Erik Miller to face the lefty-swinging Bellinger, who delivered an RBI single that put the Yankees up, 2-0.
Then in the sixth, after an intentional walk to Ben Rice in front of him, Bellinger capped a six-run rally with a three-run home run against right-handed reliever Garrett Whitlock — a 360-foot drive into the right-field stands that served as the dagger.
“He’s built for this,” Judge said Wednesday during a champagne-soaked celebration in the Yankees clubhouse. “He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment, and he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Bellinger, who won the 2019 National League MVP and the 2020 World Series with the Los Angeles Dodgers, is in his second season with the Yankees, having re-signed last winter on a five-year, $162.5 million contract.
Despite missing a month with a hamstring strain, Bellinger batted .264 with 17 home runs, 73 RBI and a .768 OPS in 132 games. He was worth 4.6 WAR (wins above replacement), in part because of his excellent defensive work in left field, too.
“This offseason, there were a couple of other teams involved,” Clay Bellinger said in August of his son’s free agency. “But I said, ‘If you can sign back with these guys, and you go out there and you win a world championship to add to this legacy, there’s no better place in the world to play baseball.’”
The elder Bellinger would know, as the former utility player won World Series with the Yankees in 1999 and 2000.
Now, the Yankees’ World Series aspirations rest in large part with Bellinger, who continues to carve out his own pinstriped legacy.
Despite hitting left-handed, Bellinger is actually better against left-handed pitching than he is against righties, making his bat even more crucial for balance in a Judge-less lineup that’s loaded with lefties.
The Yankees went 15-for-35 (.429) against left-handers in the Red Sox series, with Bellinger recording two hits in those matchups and another top-of-the-order lefty batter in Rice totaling three.
“No secret sauce,” Bellinger said of his reverse splits. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. Felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, didn’t hear too much about the match-ups. I was just playing baseball.”
After hitting .214 in his first postseason with the Yankees, Bellinger is off to a .333 start to this one. Wednesday’s home run was Bellinger’s 11th in the postseason and his second in nine playoff games with the Yankees.
“I feel like I was able to enjoy that one,” Bellinger said. “Just a home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play. And hopefully we get many, many more this month.”

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Red Sox Paid a Massive Price for Adley Rutschman to Win in October. Then They Went 0-2
item.dc:creator: Gary Adornato
item.description: Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October. Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman. They didn’t need him to save their season. They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention. And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang
item.content:encoded:
Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

item.title: [MLB.com] Padres get revenge with commanding sweep of Cubs in Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park.
All summer, Sheets had been playing through a nasty injury -- a plantar plate tear in his left foot. He wondered if he’d be able to contribute at all. There was certainly no way he could contribute defensively.
But maybe … just maybe … if Sheets could heal just enough … he could deliver a meaningful swing or two in the postseason.
A swing like this one.
Sheets came off the bench to deliver the swing that broke the Cubs in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series on Wednesday night -- a pinch-hit, two-run home run that sent Petco Park into delirium and the Padres on course for Milwaukee.
With their 4-1 victory over the Cubs, San Diego secured a trip to the NL Division Series against the Brewers, beginning on Saturday night. But first, the Padres staged a party in the home clubhouse at Petco Park.
Before the champagne was popped and the cigars were lit, manager Craig Stammen stood at the center of it all.
“We had 13 bricks to lay,” Stammen said. “Two down, 11 more to go.”
The next three almost certainly won’t come quite so easily. For the fourth time in seven seasons, the Padres are headed to the NLDS, where they’ll meet Milwaukee in a playoff series for the first time. The Brewers own the sport’s best record. Jacob Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner, takes the ball first.
“We know who they’re throwing Game 1,” said Xander Bogaerts. “So let’s celebrate today. And then be ready for that fastball.”
Call it sweet revenge for the Padres after their 2025 season came to an end with a Wild Card Series exit at Wrigley Field.
They made quick work of the Cubs, dispatching them in two games that were never all that close. The two teams played 18 innings at Petco Park this week. The Padres led after 17 of them. The Chicago offense, which scored more runs than any other team during the regular season, was held to one across two playoff games.
“We just didn't play well enough,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “And they're playing really well.”
In Game 1, the Padres were a force of nature. The ballpark partied from the very first pitch (a Michael King fastball past Pete Crow-Armstrong) to the very last pitch (Joe Musgrove punctuating his triumphant return to the mound with a game-ending strikeout). They won, 8-0.
“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Manny Machado, a veteran of eight postseasons, said of the home crowd this week. “That was huge.”
Game 2 brought a different kind of postseason energy. A party, to be sure. But one with some tension mixed in. October baseball, on the final day of September.
San Diego jumped in front in the second with Bogaerts’ RBI single and Ethan Salas’ sacrifice fly. (Salas, the youngest player in history to catch a postseason game, also became the youngest player at any position with a postseason sac fly -- since at least 1954 when that stat was fully tracked.)
But the Cubs scratched a run back against Nick Pivetta in the fourth and worked their way into the Padres’ bullpen. Crow-Armstrong and the top of the lineup loomed in the fifth.
There were two outs and a runner aboard, and Counsell had gone with right-hander Daniel Palencia. Sheets strode to the on-deck circle, then, eventually, the batter’s box -- with those three familiar thuds echoing through the Petco Park sound system.
HO-LY SHEETS.
“You just get ready for that moment, so when it happens you don’t feel like it’s sped up on you,” Sheets said. “To see this fanbase the whole entire time, I just wanted to get in front of them, I wanted to play. These guys brought it.”
This was the moment the Padres had been planning for. When Sheets is right, he mashes right-handed pitching. He’s a weapon in the clutch and can be a force off the bench.
“We had talked about that move, probably more than I care to admit in my office, with our pro scouting and advanced scouting,” Stammen said. “We felt like Gavin was a good matchup for some of their right-handed pitching. … That’s why we put him on the bench today, just in case he could pop one like that in a big situation.
“Doesn’t always work out that way. But he made us all look good.”
In the end, Sheets would take all of one swing across two games in the series. He made it count.
Palencia threw a 100.8 mph fastball at the bottom of the zone on the inner half. Sheets turned on it -- the hardest pitch any Padre has ever homered on, regular or postseason.
“That’s Dairy Bonds, baby,” said Jackson Merrill, between puffs of a cigar in a raucous Padres clubhouse. “That’s what he does -- 101, down and in. You just don’t see that. That was sick. That was one of the cooler home runs I’ve ever seen.”
And then get ready for that fastball.

item.title: [MLB.com] Phillies vs. Braves NL Wild Card Series Game 3 FAQ (8 ET, NBC/Peacock)
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman; Todd Zolecki; Paul Casella
item.description: In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023. “Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a lit
item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

item.title: [MLB.com] Red Sox turned away by Yanks in Wild Card Series for 2nd straight year
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame. The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of la
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame.
The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series (also against the Yankees).
But the Bronx Bombers made the short burst of momentum from Contreras feel insignificant when they erupted for six runs in a game-breaking, series-breaking bottom of the sixth inning that sent deafening roars throughout Yankee Stadium and the Red Sox to a 9-2 loss on Wednesday. Those reverberating sounds were a harsh reminder to the Red Sox that this was likely to be their last game of 2026.
With two flat performances in the final two nights of September, during which they were outscored, 18-2, the Red Sox were denied a chance to play in October. It also extended the streak to five straight seasons of no postseason baseball at Fenway Park.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series, and that ended for us tonight,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So it's frustrating. And there's a lot of things you can say, but in the moment, right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it's going to take some time to get over that.”
It will go down as a roller-coaster spring, summer and brief autumn in Boston. There was the 32-46 hole, which the Sox somehow dug out of with a season-altering 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 7 that included a franchise-tying winning streak of 15 games.
Then there was the final month of the regular season, which included injuries to key players and a stunning lack of offense, two themes that carried into the postseason.
“I'm proud of what we accomplished,” said veteran starter Sonny Gray, who took the loss. “Sour taste in your mouth for the ending. But we were left for dead there for a while, and I will definitely remember that run that we went on and what that felt like, because I've never experienced anything like that in my career -- to dig ourselves out of that hole and to put ourselves in this situation, that was a lot of fun.”
For the Red Sox, the fun ended in New York before it even started.
Quite simply, very little went right for the Sox in this two-game sweep at the hands of their rivals, which lacked the drama of last year’s set that went the distance (also won by the Yankees).
“For our season to end the same way that it did last year against our biggest rival, it sucks” said Red Sox lefty Garrett Crochet.
The bottom of the sixth served as a microcosm of the futility and frustration -- the inning that deep-sixed Tracy and his club.
With Contreras creating some energy in the Boston dugout, Tracy tried to add to it by bringing on Crochet for his first appearance in a game since April 25.
Crochet’s quest to get back in time for postseason play after left shoulder woes was a compelling storyline for the Red Sox, but one that didn’t work in real time.
The lefty seemed to get off to a solid start when he struck out Spencer Jones on a sweeper. But catcher Adley Rutschman’s block wasn’t a clean one, and he appeared to hesitate before throwing to first after retrieving the wild pitch. The initial call of out was overturned on replay. Jones then stole second and moved to third on Rutschman’s throwing error.
From there, things devolved. Crochet didn’t get an out and was charged with four runs, though only one of the three hits he allowed was well-struck.
“Personally, to think that I busted my [butt] the past five months, and for it to end that way, on a personal note, it's tough,” said Crochet. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best I could, and I let them down.”
Gray turned in a strong enough start for the Sox, giving up six hits over 4 2/3 innings and leaving with his team down 1-0.
But the offense never quite came around, and the bullpen had a second straight spotty night. And just like that, the season was over.
“Obviously disappointed,” said shortstop Trevor Story. “A lot of thoughts. Proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the [criticism] and everything around, the way this team came together, and really turned the season around to get back into this position is something that was special, and we're not going to forget that. Obviously, it's not about doing amazing things in the regular season. It’s about the postseason.”

item.dc:creator: FOX Wilmington
item.description: Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3. The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error. item.content:encoded:
Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3.
The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Andrew Painter then took over. The regular-season starter worked three scoreless innings to protect Philadelphia’s taxed bullpen, stranded two runners in the 10th and struck out Dominic Smith after the Phillies won an ABS challenge.
Playing under traditional extra-inning rules that don’t include designated runners at second base like in the regular season, Bohm delivered his third career postseason home run, a 357-foot shot to right field off right-hander Didier Fuentes.
The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday’s Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.
In the seventh, Drake Baldwin’s double glanced off Harper’s glove in right field, driving in Sean Murphy to give Atlanta a 2-1 lead. Harper, who resumed playing the outfield late this season for the first time since 2022, got a poor jump and was leaping for the ball near the warning track. He was not charged with an error. Matt Olson added a sacrifice fly.
“Probably should have been caught, obviously,” Harper said.
The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves‘ 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.
Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.

Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6.2 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.
The start time for the decisive Game 3 has not yet been determined. The Braves announced that MLB will schedule the game for either 2:15 p.m. ET or 8:15 p.m. ET in Atlanta, with the final time dependent on the conclusion of the other three Wild Card Series Game 2 matchups tonight.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: [mlb.com] Houston? No problem! White Sox end 21-year wait with sweep
item.dc:creator: Scott Merkin

item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- There was a moment with nobody out in the sixth inning Wednesday night during Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series that perfectly encapsulated the White Sox remarkable season and the downright fun they’ve had along the way.
Chase Meidroth connected on a three-run home run off Bryan Abreu, turning a one-run lead into a 7-3 advantage, which was ultimately the final score. But it was Meidroth’s reaction that reinforced the point.
Meidroth pumped his fist and screamed with joy from the moment he connected until he touched home plate, his emotions on full display. Back in the visitors’ clubhouse, the champagne was chilling as the White Sox prepared to take another somewhat unexpected step in the postseason.
“When I’m locked in on the field, I don’t know what goes through my mind,” Meidroth said. “All I’m thinking about is me and the baseball and trying to compete. But I had a good feeling.”
Good feelings have surrounded the White Sox since Spring Training, even dating back to SoxFest in late January. They’ve arguably been baseball’s best story in 2026, and perhaps one of the best in sports.
But this two-game sweep against the undermanned Astros proved they are a talented team to be reckoned with throughout the postseason. They are more than the young, energetic squad that shook off three consecutive 100-plus-loss campaigns to reach the playoffs.
Their second clubhouse celebration in a week -- and one of five they hope to have this postseason -- marked their first playoff series victory since 2005. That last series victory was a four-game sweep over the Astros in the World Series, with Games 3 and 4 played at what is now Daikin Park.
“These players are scared of nothing,” White Sox general manager Chris Getz said. “And whether it be myself or others, it’s like, 'How do we continue to nurture and fuel this group?'”
"We were able to do that with two games that I thought were emblematic of how we've won all season,” manager Will Venable said. “Contributions from everywhere. Sammy [Antonacci] setting the tone, great job down the lineup with everyone behind him. Guys pitching in different spots, going out whenever and getting the job done, and they did it."
For the second straight game, Chicago took control in the first inning with the help of Houston's poor defense. The White Sox scored four runs off Astros ace Hunter Brown, who had a 6-0 record with a 2.39 ERA over six career starts against the White Sox entering Wednesday.
Antonacci doubled on a line drive to left field that Yordan Alvarez seemed to have a play on but didn’t make. Kyle Teel singled home Antonacci, and Miguel Vargas reached on third baseman Nick Allen’s fielding error.
Andrew Benintendi singled home a second run, and when Lucas Spence's throw home got away from catcher Yainer Diaz, Vargas scored the third run. Tristan Peters then added an RBI single to cap the scoring in the opening frame.
Houston crept back with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve off White Sox ace Sean Burke, who struck out eight over four innings. The Astros had a golden opportunity in the fifth inning, putting runners on first and second with one out for Alvarez. Anthony Kay was on the mound for his first true relief appearance this season.
Kay fell behind in the count, 3-0, threw a pitch in the zone that was taken by Alvarez and then got him to fly out to Antonacci in left on the next pitch. Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases, but Altuve flied out to right to end the frame.
Then Meidroth provided breathing room in the sixth, launching his three-run homer to restore Chicago’s four-run lead. Twelve outs stood between the White Sox and playoff history, but they had reasserted control, and Erick Fedde handled the final two innings to finish it off.
“You saw how it was this series,” Kay said. “Everyone didn't worry about themselves, just played as a team and did the best they could.”
“Hard to imagine myself in that situation, honestly, but I'm so glad they chose me with the ball and to give the team the win,” Fedde said. “This whole fan base deserved [this]. This whole organization deserved [this]. Feels good to move on to the next round.”
And now, it’s on to Cleveland and the AL Division Series for the White Sox, in the ongoing saga between AL Central rivals. The White Sox won the season series, 7-6, but the Guardians won the division by one game to earn home-field advantage.
Cleveland features a strong rotation and one of the best closers in the game in Cade Smith. Then again, the Guardians will see a team on a roll that has been 21 years in the making.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bullpen stung by long ball after Mahle's strong playoff debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength. “I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] PCA, Cubs meekly exit playoffs after offense disappears in 2-game Wild Card sweep by Padres
